Ant body size is also partly related to thermoregulation, as larger bodies enable organisms to lose heat slower than smaller bodied organisms, and larger organisms would be expected in cooler, canopied environments. This was observed in Zululand, with smaller individuals in grassland compared to the wooded biotopes. However, the opposite trend was seen in the Midlands. Body size, however, also relates to manoeuvrability in the environment, with smaller bodies being more beneficial in more complex environments (Farji-Brener et al., 2004). This may have explained the prevalence of large-bodied ants in the grassland. Although it is difficult to say with certainty how arthropods perceive the complexity of the studied vegetation types, the grassland generally had greater bare ground cover, less leaf litter cover, and less dead wood cover than the wooded biotopes in both regions (Table S6), suggesting that the litter and topsoil layer in grassland may be less structurally complex for the focal organisms. Regarding femur length, several studies suggest ground cover complexity is correlated to femur lengths (Wiescher et al., 2012), with shorter femur lengths being more beneficial in more complex environments. Long legs were observed in the grasslands and short legs in eucalypt compartments in Zululand, corresponding with the expected pattern if the grassland soil surface is perceived as structurally simpler than in plantations. We observed no association between femur length and habitat type in the Midlands.
